title: Giving Help and Living Longer
text:
It is widely accepted that receiving support from others is good for health. In 2003 Stephanie Brown, Randolph Nesse, Amiram Vinokur and Dylan Smith of the University of Michigan asked whether giving support might matter too.

They used data from a study of older married couples in the Detroit area. At the start, the participants were asked how much practical help they gave to friends, relatives and neighbors, such as transportation, errands and childcare, and how much emotional support they gave to their spouse. They were also asked how much help they received. The researchers then followed them for five years and recorded who died.

People who reported giving more help were significantly less likely to die during those five years. The link remained after accounting for age, sex, health, income and many other factors. Receiving help, on the other hand, showed no protective link once these were considered. The authors suggested that the benefits of close relationships may come partly from what we give, not only from what we get. Contributing to others' lives may bring purpose and connection that are good for the giver's own health.
lesson: Helping others may be as good for you as being helped. Look for regular, practical ways to be useful to the people around you.
people: Stephanie Brown, Randolph Nesse, Amiram Vinokur, Dylan Smith
source: Brown, S. L., Nesse, R. M., Vinokur, A. D., and Smith, D. M. (2003). Providing social support may be more beneficial than receiving it: Results from a prospective study of mortality. Psychological Science, 14(4), 320-327.
caveat: The study is observational, so it cannot fully rule out that healthier people are simply more able to give help.
